newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia commemorates victims of fascist camp.
newsitem.headline: Croatia commemorates victims of fascist camp.

text.p: Clerics of four religions held an ecumenical service attended by several Croatian leaders on Sunday to commemorate victims of a Croatian fascist concentration camp.

Tens of thousands of Serbs, Jews, gypsies and Croatian anti-fascists died in the Jasenovac camp run by Croatia's Nazi puppet "Ustasha" regime in World War Two. A flower-shaped monument to the victims was later built at the site.
The memorial service in the crypt of the monument marked the 52nd anniversary of the camp's dissolution as fascist rule collapsed in April 1945 and 50 inmates escaped.
Victims of Ustasha terror, their families and veterans of the Partisan movement that fought the Ustasha have long held commemorations at the camp.

Leaders of Croatia's nationalist government who attended this year included Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa, Economy Minister Nenad Porges, who is Jewish, and the head of the presidential cabinet, Hrvoje Sarinic.
A wreath was laid on behalf of President Franjo Tudjman and his government.
About 500 people including foreign diplomats took part in the service conducted by Roman Catholic Croat, Serb Christian Orthodox, Jewish and Slav Moslem clerics.
A choir sang a well-known song of communist Partisan fighters from World War Two.

"Let Jasenovac and the suffering of this camp's inmates remain a permanent warning to mankind, so that this tragedy never happens again," state radio quoted the head of Croatia's small Jewish community, Ognjen Kraus, as saying.

Jasenovac, near the Bosnian border 100 km (65 miles) southeast of Zagreb, is in region seized by minority Serbs in a 1991 revolt against Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia but recaptured two years ago.

The monument was built by the late Communist leader of old federal Yugoslavia, Marshal Tito, who as head of the Partisans battled Nazi Germany's invasion army, the Ustasha and Serb ultra-rightist "Chetniks" during World War Two.

When Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia, Jews, Serbs and human rights groups accused Tudjman and his nationalist party of re-introducing Ustasha symbols and trying to whitewash Ustasha crimes.
Tudjman was also criticised by Jews and others for a 1996 proposal, since shelved, to build a new memorial centre at Jasenovac "reuniting" the remains of victims and perpetrators.

His nationalist government has denied trying to foster a revival of fascist ideology, saying the symbols in question dated from mediaeval Croatia. Tudjman has also apologised to world Jewry for perceived insensitivity.
